Which of the following properties of the alkaline earth metals increase from Be to Ba?

(i) Atomic radius (ii) Ionisation energy (iii) Nuclear charge
question:
Which of the following properties of the alkaline earth metals increase from Be to Ba?

(i) Atomic radius (ii) Ionisation energy (iii) Nuclear charge
solution:
When we go down in Group 2 (alkaline earth metals) from Beryllium (Be) to Barium (Ba), this is the trend which followed:

i. Atomic radius:

Going down Group 2 ($\mathrm{Be} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca} \rightarrow \mathrm{Sr} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ba}$), each element adds a new electron shell.

When a new shell is added, it increases the distance between the nucleus and the outermost

electrons, so the atomic radius increases.

Increases

ii. Ionisation energy:

Although the nuclear charge increases down the group, the atomic radius increases more

significantly, and there is increased shielding from inner electron shells.

So, overall, removing the outermost electron becomes easier. Hence, the ionisation energy

decreases from Be to Ba.

Not increases

iii. Nuclear charge:

Moving down the group means moving to elements with higher atomic number, i.e., more

protons in the nucleus. Since Nuclear charge is simply the number of protons, it increases

consistently from Be ($Z=4$) to Ba ($Z=56$).

Increases

We have (i) and (iii) as increasing, therefore our answer is B.

Answer: B

question:
The 1st, 2nd and the 3rd ionization enthalpies $I_1$, $I_2$ and $I_3$, of four atoms with atomic numbers n, n + 1, n + 2 and n + 3, where $n \lt 10$, are tabulated below. What is the value of n?

Atomic NumberIonization Enthalpy (kJ/mol)
$I_1$$I_2$$I_3$
n157933746043
n + 1207539526125
n + 249345626907
n + 373914517731
solution:
The key to solving this problem is to look for sudden, massive jumps in successive ionization enthalpies (IE), which indicate the removal of an electron from a highly stable noble gas core.

  • Atom n + 2: There is a massive jump between the first ($I_1 = 493\ \text{kJ/mol}$) and second ($I_2 = 4562\ \text{kJ/mol}$) ionization enthalpies. This indicates the atom has exactly 1 valence electron, making it an Alkali Metal (Group 1).
  • Atom n + 3: There is a huge jump between the second ($I_2 = 1451\ \text{kJ/mol}$) and third ($I_3 = 7731\ \text{kJ/mol}$) ionization enthalpies. This indicates it has exactly 2 valence electrons, making it an Alkaline Earth Metal (Group 2).
  • Atom n + 1: This atom has the highest first ionization enthalpy of the group ($I_1 = 2075\ \text{kJ/mol}$). Extremely high first ionization energies are characteristic of completely filled shells, meaning it is a Noble Gas (Group 18).

Let's match these properties to atomic numbers ($Z$) on the periodic table, keeping in mind the condition $n \lt 10$:

  • The alkali metal (atom n + 2) with $I_1 \approx 493\ \text{kJ/mol}$ is Sodium (Na), which has an atomic number of $11$.
  • The noble gas right before it (atom n + 1) is Neon (Ne), which has an atomic number of $10$. This perfectly aligns with the very high $I_1$ of $2075\ \text{kJ/mol}$.
  • The alkaline earth metal right after it (atom n + 3) is Magnesium (Mg), which has an atomic number of $12$.

Since we established that atom $n + 2$ has an atomic number of $11$:

n + 2 = 11

n = 9

We can verify this: if $n = 9$, the atom is Fluorine (F), which naturally sits right before Neon ($n + 1 = 10$). Its sequence of ionization enthalpies correctly fits a halogen.

Therefore, the value of $n$ is 9, which corresponds to Option D.

If a monovalent positive ion of A, a divalent positive ion of B, and a trivalent positive ion of C have zero electrons. Then the incorrect order of the corresponding I.E. is :
question:
Consider the following ionisation reactions :

If a monovalent positive ion of A, a divalent positive ion of B, and a trivalent positive ion of C have zero electrons. Then the incorrect order of the corresponding I.E. is :
solution:
• $A^+$ has 0 electrons $\implies$ Neutral A has 1 electron. Therefore, A is Hydrogen (H).
  • $B^{2+}$ has 0 electrons $\implies$ Neutral B has 2 electrons. Therefore, B is Helium (He).
  • $C^{3+}$ has 0 electrons $\implies$ Neutral C has 3 electrons. Therefore, C is Lithium (Li).
  • $A_1$: I.E. of H ($1s^1 \rightarrow 1s^0$).
  • $B_1$: 1st I.E. of He.   $B_2$: 2nd I.E. of He ($\mathrm{He}^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{He}^{2+}$).
  • $C_1$: 1st I.E. of Li.   $C_2$: 2nd I.E. of Li.   $C_3$: 3rd I.E. of Li ($\mathrm{Li}^{2+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Li}^{3+}$).
  • Option A ($C_3 \gt B_2 \gt A_1$): These represent the I.E. of single-electron (hydrogen-like) species: $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$, $\mathrm{He}^+$, and $\mathrm{H}$. For such species, I.E. $\propto Z^2$. Since nuclear charge $Z$ follows $\mathrm{Li} (3) \gt \mathrm{He} (2) \gt \mathrm{H} (1)$, the order $C_3 \gt B_2 \gt A_1$ is absolutely correct.
  • Option B ($B_1 \gt A_1 \gt C_1$): These are the first I.E. values for He, H, and Li. Helium has a highly stable $1s^2$ noble gas configuration (highest I.E.). Lithium has a shielded $2s^1$ electron, making it the easiest to remove. Hydrogen is in between. So, $\mathrm{He} \gt \mathrm{H} \gt \mathrm{Li}$ is correct.
  • Option C ($C_3 \gt C_2 \gt B_2$): Successive ionization energies always increase for the same element, so $C_3 \gt C_2$ is a given. Furthermore, $C_2$ (removing an electron from $\mathrm{Li}^+$ with $Z=3$) requires more energy than $B_2$ (removing from $\mathrm{He}^+$ with $Z=2$). This order is correct.
  • Option D ($B_2 \gt C_3 \gt A_1$): As established in Option A, $C_3$ ($\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$) is strictly greater than $B_2$ ($\mathrm{He}^+$) due to a higher nuclear charge pulling on that single remaining electron. Therefore, stating $B_2 \gt C_3$ is completely incorrect.

Since the question asks for the incorrect order, the correct choice is Option D.

question:
Outermost electronic configuration of four elements A, B, C and D are given below.

(A) [Ne] $3s^2 3p^1$

(B) [Ne] $3s^2 3p^2$

(C) [Ne] $3s^2 3p^3$

(D) [Ar] $3d^{10} 4s^2 4p^3$

The correct order of first ionisation enthalpy for them is
solution:
• (A) $[\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2 3p^1$: Aluminum (Al) – Group 13, Period 3
  • (B) $[\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2 3p^2$: Silicon (Si) – Group 14, Period 3
  • (C) $[\mathrm{Ne}]\, 3s^2 3p^3$: Phosphorus (P) – Group 15, Period 3
  • (D) $[\mathrm{Ar}]\, 3d^{10} 4s^2 4p^3$: Arsenic (As) – Group 15, Period 4

General Rules:

  1. IE generally increases across a period (left to right) due to increasing effective nuclear charge.
  2. IE generally decreases down a group (top to bottom) due to the increasing atomic size and shielding effect.
  3. Elements with exactly half-filled or fully-filled orbitals are extra stable and require significantly higher energy to remove an electron.

1. Across Period 3 (A, B, C):

Following the general trend across a period, the order should be Al < Si < P. Moreover, Phosphorus (C) has a stable exactly half-filled $p$-orbital ($3p^3$), which makes its first ionization enthalpy exceptionally high. Thus, A < B < C.

2. Down Group 15 (C vs. D):

Both Phosphorus (C) and Arsenic (D) have stable half-filled configurations ($ns^2 np^3$). However, as we move down the group from P to As, the atomic radius increases, and the outermost electrons are further from the nucleus. Therefore, it is easier to remove an electron from As than from P. Thus, D < C.

3. Comparing B (Si) and D (As):

Although As (D) is in a lower period than Si (B), the extra stability of the half-filled $4p^3$ configuration in Group 15 makes its ionization energy higher than that of Group 14's Silicon ($3p^2$). Thus, B < D.

Putting it all together: Aluminum has the lowest, Phosphorus has the highest, and Arsenic is greater than Silicon due to its half-filled stability.

Final Order: A < B < D < C

Therefore, the correct choice is Option A.

q: Which one of the following statements is incorrect in relation to ionisation enthalpy?
question: Which one of the following statements is incorrect in relation to ionisation enthalpy?
options: Ionization enthalpy increases for each successive electron.
The greatest increase in ionization enthalpy is experienced on removal of electron from core of noble gas configuration.
End of valence electrons is marked by a big jump in ionization enthalpy.
Removal of electron from orbitals bearing lower n value is easier than from orbitals having higher n value.
solution:
• Option A (Correct Statement): Ionization enthalpy always increases for successive electrons ($IE_1 \lt IE_2 \lt IE_3 \dots$). This is because as each electron is removed, the ion becomes more positive, increasing the effective nuclear charge pulling on the remaining electrons and making them harder to remove.
  • Option B (Correct Statement): Noble gas configurations represent highly stable, completely filled, closed-shell structures. Removing an electron from this tightly bound core requires an exceptionally high amount of energy.
  • Option C (Correct Statement): This is a direct consequence of the previous point. Once all loosely bound valence electrons are removed, the next electron must be pulled from an inner, stable core shell, which results in a sudden, massive jump in the required ionization energy.
  • Option D (Incorrect Statement): The principal quantum number '$n$' represents the main energy shell and its relative distance from the nucleus. Orbitals with lower '$n$' values (e.g., $n=1, 2$) are closer to the nucleus, experience less shielding, and are subject to a much stronger nuclear pull. Therefore, it is harder (not easier) to remove an electron from an orbital with a lower '$n$' value compared to a higher '$n$' value.

Conclusion:

Statement D is conceptually reversed regarding the relationship between the principal quantum number and ionization energy, making it the only incorrect statement.

Therefore, the correct choice is Option D.

solution:
Alkali metals (Group 1 elements) have a general outermost electronic configuration of $ns^1$. They readily lose this single valence electron to achieve a highly stable noble gas configuration.

Because the single valence electron is relatively far from the nucleus and easily lost, the first ionization energy, $\text{(IE)}_1$, is low.

However, once this first electron is removed, the resulting cation has a stable, closed-shell noble gas core. Removing a second electron from this tightly bound core requires a tremendous amount of energy. Therefore, the signature of an alkali metal is a massive, sudden jump between its $\text{(IE)}_1$ and $\text{(IE)}_2$ values.

Let's examine the difference between the first and second ionization energies for each element:

  • Element X: $500 \rightarrow 1000$ (increases by a factor of 2)
  • Element Y: $600 \rightarrow 2000$ (increases by a factor of ~3.3)
  • Element Z: $550 \rightarrow 7500$ (increases by a factor of ~13.6) – Massive Jump!
  • Element M: $700 \rightarrow 1400$ (increases by a factor of 2)

Element Z exhibits the characteristic enormous jump in ionization energy after the first electron is removed. This confirms that it only had one easily removable valence electron, which is the defining trait of Group 1 alkali metals.

Therefore, the correct choice is Option C.

q: Which of the following relation is correct with respect to first (I) and second (II) ionization enthalpies of potassium and calcium?
question: Which of the following relation is correct with respect to first (I) and second (II) ionization enthalpies of potassium and calcium?
solution:
• Potassium (K, atomic number 19): $[Ar]\ 4s^1$

  • Calcium (Ca, atomic number 20): $[Ar]\ 4s^2$

1. First Ionization Enthalpy ($I$)

  • Removing the first electron from Calcium requires more energy than Potassium because Calcium has a higher effective nuclear charge, and you are removing an electron from a fully-filled, stable $4s^2$ orbital.

  • Therefore, $I_{Ca} \gt I_K$ (Option B is incorrect).

2. Second Ionization Enthalpy ($II$)

  • After losing one electron, $K^+$ achieves a highly stable noble gas configuration ($[Ar]$). Removing a second electron from this stable closed-shell core requires a tremendous amount of energy.

  • After losing one electron, $Ca^+$ has the configuration $[Ar]\ 4s^1$. Removing this second electron is relatively easy because doing so allows the calcium ion to achieve a stable noble gas configuration ($Ca^{2+}$).

  • Because breaking the stable noble gas core of $K^+$ is much harder than removing the single $4s$ electron from $Ca^+$, the second ionization enthalpy of Potassium is significantly higher than that of Calcium.

  • Therefore, $II_K \gt II_{Ca}$.

This makes Option D the correct answer.

q: Which of the following represents the correct order of increasing first ionization enthalpy for Ca, Ba, S, Se and Ar?
question: Which of the following represents the correct order of increasing first ionization enthalpy for Ca, Ba, S, Se and Ar?
solution:
The first ionization enthalpy is the energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It depends on factors like atomic size, effective nuclear charge, and the stability of the electronic configuration.

1. Group Trends (Top to Bottom)

As you move down a group, the atomic size increases and the shielding effect of inner electrons becomes more prominent. This decreases the effective nuclear charge felt by the outermost electrons, making them easier to remove. Therefore, ionization enthalpy decreases down a group.

  • Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals): Barium (Ba) is below Calcium (Ca). Therefore, Ba < Ca.

  • Group 16 (Chalcogens): Selenium (Se) is below Sulfur (S). Therefore, Se < S.

2. Period Trends (Left to Right)

As you move across a period from left to right, the atomic radius decreases while the effective nuclear charge increases. This holds the valence electrons more tightly, meaning more energy is required to remove them. Therefore, ionization enthalpy generally increases across a period.

  • The metals in Group 2 (Ca, Ba) have larger atomic radii and lower effective nuclear charge compared to the non-metals in Group 16 (S, Se).

  • Therefore, the ionization enthalpies of the Group 2 metals will be strictly lower than those of the Group 16 non-metals: (Ba, Ca) < (Se, S).

3. Noble Gas Stability

Argon (Ar) is a Group 18 noble gas. It possesses a stable, fully filled valence shell configuration ($ns^2np^6$). Because of this extraordinary stability, breaking the octet requires a massive amount of energy.

  • Argon will have the highest first ionization enthalpy among all the given elements.

Final Order

Combining these rules gives us the final increasing order of first ionization enthalpy:

Ba < Ca < Se < S < Ar

Given below are two statements.

Statement I The correct order of second ionisation enthalpy values of Na, Al, Mg and Si is

Na > Mg < Al > Si.

Statement II The correct order of first ionisation enthalpies of the elements B, P, S and F is

B < S < P < F.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
question:
Given below are two statements.

Statement I The correct order of second ionisation enthalpy values of Na, Al, Mg and Si is

Na > Mg < Al > Si.

Statement II The correct order of first ionisation enthalpies of the elements B, P, S and F is

B < S < P < F.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
solution:
The second ionization enthalpy ($IE_2$) is the energy required to remove an electron from a unipositive cation ($M^+$). Let's examine the electronic configurations of the unipositive ions for these elements:

  • $Na^+$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ (Stable noble gas core)

  • $Mg^+$: $[Ne] 3s^1$

  • $Al^+$: $[Ne] 3s^2$ (Stable fully-filled s-subshell)

  • $Si^+$: $[Ne] 3s^2 3p^1$

Now, let's compare the energy required to remove the next electron:

  1. Na vs. Mg: $Na^+$ has achieved the highly stable configuration of Neon. Disrupting this noble gas core requires an exceptionally high amount of energy compared to removing the lone $3s^1$ electron from $Mg^+$. Therefore, Na > Mg.

  2. Mg vs. Al: $Al^+$ has a fully-filled $3s^2$ subshell, which offers extra stability. $Mg^+$ only has a single electron in the $3s$ orbital. Removing an electron from $Al^+$ will require more energy. Therefore, Mg < Al.

  3. Al vs. Si: For $Si^+$, the outermost electron is in the $3p$ subshell. The $3p$ subshell is higher in energy and slightly farther from the nucleus than the $3s$ subshell. Removing an electron from the $3p$ orbital of $Si^+$ is easier than breaking the stable $3s^2$ configuration of $Al^+$. Therefore, Al > Si.

Combining these observations gives the exact trend provided: Na > Mg < Al > Si.

Result: Statement I is True.

Evaluating Statement II (First Ionization Enthalpy)

We need to determine the correct order for the first ionization enthalpies ($IE_1$) of Boron (B), Phosphorus (P), Sulfur (S), and Fluorine (F). Let's look at their outer electronic configurations:

  • B: $[He] 2s^2 2p^1$

  • P: $[Ne] 3s^2 3p^3$ (Stable half-filled p-subshell)

  • S: $[Ne] 3s^2 3p^4$

  • F: $[He] 2s^2 2p^5$

Comparing their ionization enthalpies:

  1. Fluorine (F) is positioned at the top right of the periodic table (excluding noble gases). It has the smallest atomic size and the highest effective nuclear charge among these elements, making its ionization enthalpy the highest.

  2. Phosphorus (P) vs. Sulfur (S): Here we see an exception to the general left-to-right periodic trend. Phosphorus has an exactly half-filled $3p$ subshell ($3p^3$), which provides extra exchange energy and stability. Because of this, it is harder to remove an electron from Phosphorus than from Sulfur ($3p^4$). Therefore, S < P.

  3. Boron (B) is located on the far left side of the p-block in Group 13. It has a relatively low effective nuclear charge, and removing its single $2p$ electron is the easiest of the group.

Putting it all together, the increasing order is exactly B < S < P < F.

Result: Statement II is True.

Final Answer

Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

q: One element has atomic weight 39. Its electronic configuration is $1s^2, 2s^2 2p^6, 3s^2 3p^6 4s^1$. The true statement for that element is
question: One element has atomic weight 39. Its electronic configuration is $1s^2, 2s^2 2p^6, 3s^2 3p^6 4s^1$. The true statement for that element is
solution:
• Electronic Configuration: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^1$

  • Atomic Number ($Z$): By adding the number of electrons, we get $2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 1 = 19$. The element is Potassium (K).

  • Atomic Mass ($A$): The question states the atomic weight (mass number) is 39.

  • Number of Neutrons: $A - Z = 39 - 19 = 20$ neutrons.

2. Evaluate the Options:

  • Option A (high value of IE): False. The element has a single valence electron ($4s^1$), making it an alkali metal (Group 1). Alkali metals have the lowest ionization enthalpies in their respective periods because removing that one electron gives them a highly stable noble gas configuration.

  • Option B (transition element): False. The last electron enters an $s$-orbital ($4s^1$), so it is an $s$-block element, not a $d$-block (transition) element.

  • Option C (isotone with $^{38}_{18}\text{Ar}$): True. Isotones are species that have the same number of neutrons. Let's calculate the neutrons for Argon-38:

  • Number of neutrons in $^{38}_{18}\text{Ar} = 38 - 18 = 20$.

  • Since our element also has 20 neutrons, they are isotones.

  • Option D ($p$-block element): False. As established above, its outermost electron is in an $s$-orbital, making it an $s$-block element.

Final Answer

Option C: isotone with $^{38}_{18}\text{Ar}$

14.534, 29.601, 47.448, 77.472, 97.888, 552.057, 667.029

Find the number of valence shell electrons in that element.
question:
For an element the successive ionisation energy values (in eV/atom), are given below.

14.534, 29.601, 47.448, 77.472, 97.888, 552.057, 667.029

Find the number of valence shell electrons in that element.
solution:
1. Understand Successive Ionization Energies:

Successive ionization energies ($\mathrm{IE}_1, \mathrm{IE}_2, \mathrm{IE}_3, \dots$) always increase because it requires more energy to remove an electron from a progressively more positive ion.

2. Identify the "Jump":

A sudden, massive increase (a "jump") in successive ionization energy values indicates that all valence electrons have been removed, and the next electron is being removed from a stable, inner noble gas core.

Let's examine the given data (in eV/atom):

  • $\mathrm{IE}_1 = 14.534$

  • $\mathrm{IE}_2 = 29.601$

  • $\mathrm{IE}_3 = 47.448$

  • $\mathrm{IE}_4 = 77.472$

  • $\mathrm{IE}_5 = 97.888$

  • $\mathrm{IE}_6 = 552.057$ \leftarrow Massive Jump

  • $\mathrm{IE}_7 = 667.029$

3. Interpret the Jump:

The values increase relatively gradually from $\mathrm{IE}_1$ to $\mathrm{IE}_5$. However, there is a huge spike (more than a 5-fold increase) between the 5th and 6th ionization energies.

  • This indicates that removing the first 5 electrons is relatively easy as they are in the outermost (valence) shell.

  • Removing the 6th electron requires an exceptionally high amount of energy because it must be pulled from a highly stable, fully-filled inner shell.

Conclusion

Because the massive jump occurs right after the removal of the 5th electron, the element must have exactly 5 electrons in its outermost shell.

Final Answer:

5

q: Upto argon the total number of elements which have lower $\mathrm{IE}_1$ as compared to He .
question: Upto argon the total number of elements which have lower $\mathrm{IE}_1$ as compared to He .
solution:
1. Analyze Helium (He):

  • Helium has the atomic number 2 and an electronic configuration of $1s^2$.

  • Because its electrons are in the first shell ($n=1$), they are extremely close to the nucleus and experience no shielding from inner electron shells.

  • Consequently, Helium has the highest first ionization enthalpy ($\mathrm{IE}_1$) of all elements in the entire periodic table.

  1. Analyze the Given Range ("Upto Argon"):

  • "Upto Argon" includes all elements from Hydrogen (Atomic Number 1) to Argon (Atomic Number 18).

  • This gives us a total of 18 elements.

  1. Compare $\mathrm{IE}_1$ Values:

  • Since Helium holds the absolute maximum value for first ionization enthalpy, every other element in the periodic table has a lower $\mathrm{IE}_1$ than Helium.

  • Therefore, out of the first 18 elements, all of them will have a lower $\mathrm{IE}_1$ than Helium, except for Helium itself.

Calculation

  • Total elements up to Argon = 18

  • Minus Helium itself = $18 - 1 = 17$

Final Answer

17

question:
The successive ionisation energy values for an element are given below:

I. 1st ionisation energy = 410 kJ mol-1

II. 2nd ionisation energy = 820 kJ mol-1

III. 3rd ionisation energy = 1100 kJ mol-1

IV. 4th ionisation energy = 1500 kJ mol-1

V. 5th ionisation energy = 3200 kJ mol-1

Find out the number of valence electron for the atom x.
solution:
Successive ionization energies ($\mathrm{IE}_1, \mathrm{IE}_2, \mathrm{IE}_3, \dots$) always increase because more energy is required to remove an electron from a progressively more positive ion.

A sudden, significant increase (a "jump") in successive ionization energy values indicates that all outer valence electrons have been removed, and the next electron is being pulled from a highly stable, completely filled inner electron shell (noble gas core).

Let's examine the differences between the given successive ionization energies:

  • $\mathrm{IE}_1 = 410 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

  • $\mathrm{IE}_2 = 820 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Increase of $410 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$)

  • $\mathrm{IE}_3 = 1100 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Increase of $280 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$)

  • $\mathrm{IE}_4 = 1500 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Increase of $400 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$)

  • $\mathrm{IE}_5 = 3200 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (Increase of $1700 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$)

While the energy required to remove the first four electrons increases relatively gradually, there is a sudden, sharp spike between the 4th and 5th ionization energies. The energy difference more than quadruples compared to the previous step.

  • This indicates that removing the first 4 electrons is relatively easier because they belong to the outermost (valence) shell.

  • The 5th electron requires significantly more energy to remove because it must be extracted from a stable, inner principal quantum shell.

Conclusion

Because the largest jump in required energy occurs right after the removal of the 4th electron, the element must have exactly 4 electrons in its outermost shell.

Final Answer:

4

question:
How many of the following have ionisation energy greater than the Phosphorous atom?

$\begin{array}{lllll}N & O & F & N e & C l\end{array}$

S $\quad \mathrm{Si} \quad \mathrm{Al} \quad \mathrm{C}$
solution:
First, let's analyze the target element, Phosphorus (P):

  • Atomic Number: 15

  • Electronic Configuration: $[\text{Ne}] 3s^2 3p^3$

  • Phosphorus has a stable, exactly half-filled $3p$ subshell, which requires extra energy to remove an electron.

Now, let's compare the given elements with Phosphorus:

1. Elements in the same period (Period 3: Al, Si, S, Cl)

  • The general trend across a period is that ionization energy increases from left to right.

  • However, due to the half-filled stability of Phosphorus ($3p^3$), it has a higher ionization energy than Sulfur ($3p^4$).

  • The correct order for these Period 3 elements is: $\text{Al} \lt \text{Si} \lt \text{S} \lt \textbf{P} \lt \text{Cl}$

  • Greater than P: Only Cl.

2. Elements in the preceding period (Period 2: C, N, O, F, Ne)

  • Elements in Period 2 are significantly smaller in atomic size than elements in Period 3. Because their valence electrons are closer to the nucleus (in the $n=2$ shell instead of $n=3$), they experience a much stronger effective nuclear charge.

  • As a result, the ionization energies of these non-metals in Period 2 are generally much higher than those in Period 3.

  • N: Directly above P in Group 15. IE decreases down a group, so $\text{N} \gt \text{P}$.

  • O, F, Ne: Located to the right of N in Period 2, they all have very high ionization energies, substantially greater than P.

  • C: Carbon (Group 14) also has a smaller size and higher ionization energy ($\sim 1086 \text{ kJ/mol}$) compared to Phosphorus ($\sim 1011 \text{ kJ/mol}$).

  • Greater than P: C, N, O, F, Ne.

Conclusion

The elements that have an ionization energy strictly greater than Phosphorus are: N, O, F, Ne, Cl, and C.
